source: Johnson-Laird & Savary (1996) Illusory inferences about probabilities
finding: States the core theory. A conclusion is possible if it holds in at least one model, probable if it holds in most models, necessary if it holds in all models. Reasoners keep models small and write down only what is true, with implicit models marked by an ellipsis and a footnote. This yields a new prediction: illusory inferences, where the conclusion feels obvious but is wrong.
numbers: Theory section only; no numbers in this line. Two principles for relative probability: P1 proper subset of models (sound), P2 more models means more probable (risky, needs equiprobable models).
quote: A conclusion is necessary if it holds in all of the models of the premises; probable if in most; possible if in at least some.
limits: Description of the theory, written in 1995 to 1996 form. Later versions add fully explicit models and System 1 and System 2.
agent_relevance: The three-way modal rule (all models, some model, most models) is a cheap code-checkable definition of necessary, possible and probable. Code can enumerate models and count.

source: Johnson-Laird & Savary (1996) Illusory inferences about probabilities
finding: Experiment 1: illusory probability problems. Example: only one of two assertions is true (king or ace or both; queen or ace or both). Which is more likely, king or ace? Most say ace. Truth: if an ace were in the hand, both assertions would be true, so ace is impossible.
numbers: N=24 Princeton students, each did 2 illusory and 2 control problems. Correct on 71% of controls and 17% of illusions. 20 of 24 did better on controls, 2 ties, sign test p<.001. 21 of 24 picked an impossible card on at least one illusion.
limits: Small N, paper-and-pencil, one lab. Mean of 4 problems per person. Cards content only.
agent_relevance: Tests a case where a plausible chain of reasoning silently drops the false cases. A scaffold that must also list what is false in each case is the fix the theory implies.

source: Johnson-Laird & Savary (1996) Illusory inferences about probabilities
finding: Experiment 2: six illusory problems and six matched controls, with exclusive disjunction or biconditional as main connective. Illusions occurred with many connectives, not only one. Responses piled up at impossible, 50/50 and certain, matching the models. People assume equal chance for each model (indifference).
numbers: N=20 students, 12 problems each. Illusory 13% correct vs controls 64% correct (Wilcoxon T=1, n=18, p<<.005). 17 of 20 worse on illusions. All five analysed pairs in the predicted direction (sign test p<.04). Two-model controls 52% vs one-model controls 83% correct. Responses: impossible 16%, 50/50 33%, certain 34% (pooled).
limits: One problem pair dropped because the control premise was self-contradictory. Only 56% of responses on illusions matched the exact model prediction, so the theory predicts the direction better than each answer.
agent_relevance: Item difficulty tracks the number of explicit models needed (83% vs 52%). A code count of models per item could flag which items need extra enumeration.

source: Johnson-Laird & Savary (1999) Illusory inferences: a novel class of erroneous deductions
finding: Three experiments establish illusory inferences as a class and rule out several rival explanations. Example: If king then ace, or else if not king then ace; there is a king; what follows? Everyone says ace. Truth: one conditional is false, so there is no ace guarantee.
numbers: Experiment 1 (n=16): 100% of conclusions on illusions were the predicted invalid ones; every participant did better on controls (p<1 in 65,000). Mean confidence 4.4/5 on illusions and 4.3/5 on controls. Experiment 2 (web, n=20 per problem): 15 of 20 chose the illusory 'there is an ace', 5 chose indeterminate; 15 of 20 got the control right.
limits: Web experiment has no control over strategy, forced choice among 3 options allows guessing. Small samples.
agent_relevance: Confidence is the same for right and wrong answers, so an agent's own confidence cannot flag these errors. Supports G10 and the rule that checks must come from code.

source: Johnson-Laird & Savary (1999) Illusory inferences: a novel class of erroneous deductions
finding: Tests rival accounts. A warning that the problems were tricky, with think-aloud, slowed people down but they still made the fallacies. The 'or else means and' reading and the 'programming language else' reading (Rips) were tested with a rubric 'one is true and one is false'; the illusion stayed. The authors say the source is thinking about joint truth but not joint falsity.
numbers: Warning study was a small-scale replication run by a colleague (no N given in the passage read). Experiment 3 used n=40. One later passage reports 90% of participants called two cards equally probable when the right answer was different.
limits: Authors are the theory's proponents. Rips raised the alternative by personal communication, and the paper answers it with the authors' own studies.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to be careful or to expect a trick is not a fix. The fix must change the procedure: force enumeration of the false case.

source: Yang & Johnson-Laird (2000) Illusions in quantified reasoning: how to make the impossible seem possible, and vice versa
finding: Illusions extend to quantified reasoning. Example: only one of two statements is true (some of the plastic beads are not red; none of the plastic beads are red). Is it possible that none of the red beads are plastic? Most say yes; correct is no. There are illusions of possibility (look possible, are impossible) and of impossibility (look impossible, are possible).
numbers: Experiment 1, N=20: controls 90% correct, illusions 54% (about chance). Inferences of impossibility easier than possibility (z=2.72, p<.01), with an interaction showing illusions of possibility are more compelling. Experiment 2, N=20, dyadic premises: controls 93%, illusions 51%. Confidence only slightly higher on controls (mean difference .13 in Exp 1, .32 in Exp 2 on a 5-point scale). A cited rate: three quarters said yes to one problem whose correct answer was no.
limits: Illusions of impossibility were much weaker (near 54% pooled) and vary a lot by item. Wide spread across the 20 problems, so not every illusory form is equally strong.
agent_relevance: Not every predicted illusion works, so item-level tests matter. Also another reason to check any claim of the form 'this class of error is certain' with data.

source: Yang & Johnson-Laird (2000) How to eliminate illusions in quantified reasoning
finding: First effective antidote. Instruct people to work out the case where premise 1 is true and premise 2 is false, then the case where premise 2 is true and premise 1 is false. After that the gap between illusions and controls vanishes. A simple warning does nothing.
numbers: Exp 1 (one-case instruction): illusions 33% to 65% correct (z=3.27, p<.01); controls fell 93% to 79% (z=2.31, p<.01); overall 63% to 72%. Exp 2 (two-case instruction): illusions 39% to 71% correct (z=3.72, p<.001); controls fell 87% to 72% (p<.05); no reliable difference between illusions and controls after (z=0.44). Without instruction controls 93% and 87% vs illusions 33% and 39%.
quote: The difference between the illusory and the control problems disappeared when participants worked out both cases.
limits: Cost: accuracy on controls went down (93 to 79, 87 to 72), so the checking step has a price. Reviewer's worry that any re-check might help is answered only by an earlier failed warning study. Group sizes not read from the passage.
agent_relevance: The strongest direct support for an operator: make the agent state each premise true and the others false, one case at a time, and list the resulting possibilities. It improves hard items and hurts easy ones, so apply it on a signal, as G1 says.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2008) Illusory inferences about embedded disjunctions
finding: Principle of truth also yields illusions in pure disjunctions with no conditionals, which answers Rips's objection that illusions come from misreading 'if'. Embedded disjunctions such as A or else (B or else C) give illusory 'could you have both?' answers. Controls such as A or (B or C) are answered correctly.
numbers: Exp 1, N=18: illusory problems 17% (exclusive-exclusive) and 22% (inclusive-exclusive) correct; controls 100% and 78%. 16 of 18 did better on controls (binomial p<.005). Instruction to check true/false halfway (Exp 2, N=40): 1st block controls 97/94 and illusions 50/38 (instructed/uninstructed); 2nd block controls 88/92 and illusions 47/21.
limits: Instruction helped only partly (illusions 47% in the instructed group) and mainly stopped decline in the uninstructed group (38 to 21). Web study, yes/no responses.
agent_relevance: Even good instructions are weaker for embedded disjunctions. Plan for a code-side enumeration of true/false combinations rather than asking the model to remember them.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2008) Illusory inferences about embedded disjunctions
finding: Model counts do not explain the difficulty. Exclusive-exclusive and inclusive-exclusive problems have 3 models and are hard; inclusive-inclusive and exclusive-inclusive have 4 models and are easier or equal. So what makes the illusion is that the models are erroneous, not that there are many.
numbers: Models per problem: inclusive-inclusive 4, exclusive-inclusive 4, exclusive-exclusive 3, inclusive-exclusive 3. Correct on the 3-model illusions 17% and 22%, on the 4-model controls 100% and 78%.
limits: Authors note explicit questions may have let people work backwards from the question, avoiding full model building (cites Garcia-Madruga et al. 2001).
agent_relevance: Difficulty for a language model may not scale with the number of cases either. Test on items where more cases are right and fewer cases are wrong.

source: Johnson-Laird (2010) Mental models and human reasoning, PNAS
finding: Summary of the theory by its founder: reasoners build iconic models of possibilities, kept small by working memory; the principle of truth; fully explicit models only when forced; a counterexample search triggered when a conclusion seems unbelievable. Content shapes both interpretation and the search.
numbers: Illusory set: 15% correct vs controls 91%. Card problem with king/queen/jack-or-ten: 95% said ace possible, which is wrong. Exclusive vs inclusive disjunction conclusions: public about 20% vs under 5%; Princeton students about 75% vs under 30%. Frenchmen/gourmets: most infer 'some Frenchmen are wine-drinkers' but few infer 'some Frenchmen are Italians' for the same logical form.
quote: The key to a correct solution is to overcome the principle of truth and to envisage fully explicit models.
limits: Review by the theory's author; percentages come from cited studies not re-read here. The content-effect account (believable conclusion stops the search) is the theory's explanation, rival accounts exist.
agent_relevance: A believable first answer ends the search; an absurd one triggers it. A scaffold should run the counterexample search on every answer, not only on those that look odd to the model.

source: Johnson-Laird (2010) Mental models and human reasoning, PNAS
finding: Counterexample use in evaluating given conclusions. People are better at spotting conclusions that contradict the premises than conclusions that are only consistent with them, and they use counterexamples more in the second case.
numbers: Study of two kinds of invalid conclusion: correct rejections 92% when inconsistent with the premises vs 74% when merely consistent. Counterexample use 51% of inferences (consistent case) vs 21% (inconsistent case). Writing justifications had no reliable effect on accuracy or speed. Counterexample use correlated with accuracy.
limits: Cited summary of a study, not re-read. Correlation not causation.
agent_relevance: Detection of 'consistent but not entailed' answers is the hard case, and that is where a code-driven counterexample search adds the most (S7).

source: Johnson-Laird, Legrenzi, Girotto, Sonino Legrenzi & Caverni (1999) Naive probability: a mental model theory of extensional reasoning
finding: Naive probability theory. Without training, people infer probabilities by counting equiprobable models of what is true. Predicts typical biases and cognitive illusions in relative probability, shows subadditivity and conditional-probability errors, and handles posterior probabilities without Bayes's formula.
numbers: Experiments 1 and 2 (French-speaking students; Exp 2 n=22): predicted values like 67% for 'at least A' and 33% for A-and-B in inclusive 'A or B'. Subadditivity: 'at least A' judged 60%, but A alone 45% plus A-and-not-B 44%. Conditionals: biconditional readers' answers summed to 100% (7 of 9), conditional readers summed over 100% (7 of 8; p<.005).
limits: Participants were told to give percentages about objects in a box they knew nothing about. A reviewer doubted the sample would answer this way. Authors say Aix, Tokyo and Jerusalem students behaved alike, and the effect may not hold for people trained in probability.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete rule for how a model counts possibilities. Also shows an agent would copy the equiprobability rule unless told which cases are unequal.

source: Johnson-Laird, Legrenzi, Girotto, Sonino Legrenzi & Caverni (1999) Naive probability: a mental model theory of extensional reasoning
finding: Experiment 3: matched biased and unbiased premises. Premises whose mental models differ from the fully explicit models produce biased probability judgments; matched controls produce correct ones.
numbers: N=25. Mean 5.6 unbiased inferences out of 9 control problems but 1.1 out of 8 experimental problems. Every participant did better on controls. Matches to model-theory predictions: 5.8 of 9 (experimental) and 5.6 of 9 (control), chance 1 in 10. One control problem failed prediction (only 6 gave the unbiased value; 10 gave 50%). Fourth pair dropped for a design error.
limits: A design error removed one pair. Authors admit a pragmatic reading of one premise could explain part, though pragmatic theories do not predict the 'only what is true' pattern.
agent_relevance: Probability answers from a model that lists only true cases are biased. Code that expands the full state table and counts gives the unbiased answer.

source: Johnson-Laird, Legrenzi, Girotto, Sonino Legrenzi & Caverni (1999) Naive probability: a mental model theory of extensional reasoning
finding: A cue that forces separate counting of denominator and numerator rescues Bayesian-style answers. Girotto and Gonzalez had people fill in 'out of 10 chances, N have the symptom; among these, M are associated with the disease'.
numbers: 53% correct with this instruction vs 8% on a control problem (as cited in the paper).
limits: Cited from another study. Works because integer chances give easy subset models; paper says problems with non-integer numbers break this.
agent_relevance: Format the task as counted cases in code (integers out of a total), then let the model read off the subset. This matches the 'code counts, model fills slot' split.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis
finding: Meta-analysis of 12 syllogism theories against data from 6 studies. None is adequate. The mental model program predicts too many conclusions (high hit rate, low correct rejection). The verbal-models theory gave the best balance. Aggregated model theories beat heuristic theories.
numbers: Hits: mental models 95%, verbal models 63%, matching 59%, PHM 52%, atmosphere 51%, PSYCOP 44%, conversion 44%. Correct rejections: conversion 93%, verbal 90%, atmosphere 85%, PSYCOP 85%, PHM 79%, mental models 74%, matching 74%. Overall correct: verbal 84%, conversion 83%, mental models 78%, atmosphere 78%, PSYCOP 77%, PHM 73%, matching 71%. Model-based theories 76% vs heuristic 66% when aggregated. Verbal models predictions were marginally heterogeneous (I2=52%, p=.06).
limits: Six studies, many from one lab, only 7 of 12 theories scored. Predictions of the older mental-model program count 'possible' conclusions, which inflates hits. A publication-bias test was significant for the matching theory (p=.04). Authors conclude: 'none of the above' is correct.
agent_relevance: The older deterministic model program is a poor predictor; the stochastic mReasoner replaced it. Warns an agent against treating one theory as true: use it as a procedure, not a claim about the truth.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis
finding: Reliability of the syllogism data: human difficulty is stable across studies and countries. Hard problems produce diverse answers. Easy ones produce one or two answers.
numbers: Kendall's W=.86 (27 valid syllogisms) and .64 (37 invalid) across six studies. Entropy correlated with accuracy r=-.52 (harder means more diverse answers); W=.45 for entropy ranks. Easiest valid syllogism 90% correct; hardest valid syllogism (All B are A, None of C is B) 1% correct, most gave 'none of C is A'. Easiest invalid 76% correct (nothing follows); hardest invalid 12% correct. Easy syllogisms elicit about 1 bit of entropy, hard ones over 2 bits.
limits: Studies from the US and Italy only, university students, mostly one lab.
agent_relevance: Diversity of answers is a free uncertainty signal: if sampled answers disagree, the item is hard. Fits G1 (doubt only on a signal).

source: Bucciarelli & Johnson-Laird (1999) Strategies in syllogistic reasoning
finding: Four experiments on syllogisms with paper and pencil and with cut-out shapes. Untrained people can build counterexamples. They use the operations the program uses (add tokens, split individuals, swap properties) but with many more interpretations and search orders than the program.
numbers: Exp 1 (n=20, no think-aloud): one-model syllogisms 80% correct (26 s), multiple-model 21% (41 s), no-valid-conclusion 50% (78 s). Exp 2 (n=20, think-aloud): 76% (31 s), 21% (51 s), 41% (52 s). 39 of 40 did better on one-model problems. Mean 8.5 correct of 20; mean 2.7 errors of the predicted type; 36 of 40 made more predicted errors than not.
limits: Only 10 of 40 gave enough protocol data to classify strategies; 6 used Euler circles sometimes; people drew one diagram even when several were possible. The program predicted fewer strategies than people showed.
agent_relevance: Multiple-model problems are exactly where answers collapse (21% correct). Operators that add tokens, split individuals and swap properties are plain code-level moves for a counterexample search.

source: Bucciarelli & Johnson-Laird (1999) Strategies in syllogistic reasoning
finding: Experiment 3: given a conclusion, build a picture with cut-out shapes that makes the premises true and the conclusion false. Untrained people can refute conclusions this way. One-model items (cannot be refuted) were answered correctly most often; among refutable items, multiple-model items were easier to refute than no-valid-conclusion items.
numbers: Sign tests over 19 participants (15 better on one-model, 3 not, 1 tie; p=.004). Correct refutations 59%; correct 'cannot refute' 71%. One-model 71%, multiple-model 70%, no-valid-conclusion 50% (16 better on multiple-model, 2 not, 1 tie; p=.001).
limits: Not predicted in advance: the order of the last two categories. Task is non-standard (external models with cut-outs).
agent_relevance: Cases with no valid conclusion are where a refutation search fails most (50%). An agent should treat 'nothing follows' as a result that needs its own search, since models avoid that answer.

source: Goodwin & Johnson-Laird (2005) Reasoning about relations
finding: Relational reasoning: people build one typical iconic model, develop their own strategies, and find integration of premises hard. Difficulty depends on integration, number of entities, and depth of the relation. Models are used with transitive, pseudo-transitive and non-transitive relations.
numbers: Pseudotransitive study 1 (cited): transitive conclusions on 98% of transitive, 72% of pseudotransitive, 8% of non-transitive problems. Study 2 (n=30): 91%, 52%, 3%, with context lowering pseudotransitive inference. Strategies in think-aloud: ternary 49%, transitive 24%, frame 17% (rest other). Depth: second-order problems 84% correct vs third-order 56% (z=3.00, p<.005). Shallow vs deep problems 91% vs 93% correct (no difference).
limits: Strategies depend on how premises are presented (ternary-first order gave ternary strategy on 54% of trials vs 26% with colour coding). Experiment sizes not all read.
agent_relevance: Depth, not the count of arguments, hurts. For relational puzzles, build the order explicitly in code and give the model one integration step at a time.

source: Byrne (1989) Suppressing valid inferences with conditionals
finding: Valid conditional inferences can be suppressed by context. An extra requirement ('if she has enough money then she will go to a play') makes people withdraw modus ponens and modus tollens; an alternative cause ('if she meets her family...') withdraws the fallacies instead. Interpretation of premises matters, which is the model-theory account of how premises are turned into models.
numbers: Exp 1 (n=24, three groups of 8): modus ponens 96% simple vs 37.5% with additional antecedent; modus tollens 92% vs 33%; denial of antecedent 46% vs 4% with alternative; affirmation of consequent 71% vs 12.5% with alternative. Overall 76% simple, 52% alternative, 47% additional. Exp 2 (24 participants, 8 per group): no effect when categorical premise names both antecedents (70%, 86%, 80%; F(2,21)=1.05). Exp 3 (n=24): long-duration information lowered denial of antecedent 44% to 19%.
limits: Eight per cell, three items each. Byrne's own account is about interpretation; formal rule theorists (Braine) reply with pragmatics, not covered here.
agent_relevance: Valid rules are not applied blind; extra background content changes what the models are. A scaffold's S1 must keep the stated premises intact and not add hidden conditions.

source: Ragni & Johnson-Laird (2018) Reasoning about possibilities: human reasoning violates all normal modal logics
finding: Reasoning about possibility. People accept inferences that are invalid in modal logic when they are parsimonious (a premise establishes some possibilities, nothing beyond), and reject ones that modal logic allows but the premises do not support.
numbers: Exp 1 (n=53): model theory r2=.99 with results vs modal logic K r2=.01. People gave 80% of the predicted evaluations of model theory vs 56% for modal logic (z=6.1). Exp 2 (n=50): r2=.98 vs .05; 83% vs 50%. Where theory and logic split and theory said Yes: 89% yes (vs 11%). Where theory said No: 76% no (vs 24%).
limits: Online studies; authors are the theory's proponents; accepted inferences are 'invalid' only against standard modal logics, not against everyday meaning.
agent_relevance: People (and likely models) reason about 'could be' by listing what was stated and not beyond it. A check can be that every claimed possibility is listed by code from the premises.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2022) Reasoning about properties: a computational theory (mReasoner)
finding: mReasoner, the main computational model. System 1 builds one small model from an intensional representation and scans it with heuristics; System 2 searches for counterexamples by adding tokens, splitting an individual or swapping properties, then may revise to a weaker conclusion. Four parameters: size, atypicality, search probability, reconclude probability.
numbers: Fits data from over 200 kinds of inference; 11 simulations. Syllogism fit to the aggregated data r=.80, RMSE=.13. Johnson-Laird & Steedman (1978) 20 participants: best individual fits mean r=.70; NVC response 45% there vs 30% in other studies. Three subgroups fits r=.78, .83, .91. Only 4 free parameters; earlier simulations used dozens (Polk & Newell; Hattori).
limits: A fit to existing data, not a test on new data in all cases. Over-predicts 'no valid conclusion' slightly; flaws in predictions about absence of a property (cited). Open code on OSF.
agent_relevance: A concrete two-stage design: fast single answer, then a code-run counterexample search triggered with some probability. Matches our S3, S4, S7 pipeline and the 'search only on signal' rule.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2022) Reasoning about properties: a computational theory (mReasoner)
finding: The size parameter shows that fewer entities in the model fit better; the best parameter values vary by study. Humans are parsimonious: dozens of models do no better.
numbers: Size is a left-truncated Poisson with mean below 6; some simulations best at size above 4.0, others 2.0. Atypicality best below .5. Fitting used grid searches: for example 1,000 parameter settings x 100 runs of 32 immediate inferences, and 1,512 settings for syllogism subsamples.
limits: The grid search chooses parameters per data set, so 'fit' includes selection. Differences between studies are interpreted as ability differences, not tested.
agent_relevance: Individual differences can be cast as a search probability: some reasoners rarely check. For an agent the equivalent is a budget on counterexample searches.

source: Khemlani, Lotstein & Johnson-Laird (2014) A mental model theory of set membership
finding: Set-membership inferences (Amy is an artist, so is she a bohemian?). One-model inferences easy, multiple-model hard. mReasoner's search parameter fit at .58.
numbers: One-model 92% vs multiple-model 51% correct (Wilcoxon z=3.21, p=.001, Cliff's delta .56). 'None of the X' 83% vs 'All of the X' 72% (z=2.17, p=.03). Only one-vs-multiple models was a significant predictor in a mixed-effects model (b=3.31, SE=.42, p<.0001). Eight inferences ranged 47% to 95% correct. 9.5% of responses were qualified with a modal word. Simulation R2=.75, RMSE=.11 at search=.58.
limits: Eight inferences only, so the R2 rests on 8 data points. 'Search' parameter is fit post hoc.
agent_relevance: The one parameter that matters is whether a counterexample is searched for; a 58% search rate matched people. For an LLM the search rate could be set by difficulty (G12).

source: Johnson-Laird (2010) Mental models and human reasoning, PNAS
finding: Working memory limit: people prefer to think about just one possibility. The most frequent conclusions in a study of disjunctive premises were those consistent with a single model. Diagrams help only when they are iconic.
numbers: Conclusions drawn from pairs of exclusive vs inclusive disjunctions: accuracy fell from about 20% to under 5% (general public) and from about 75% to under 30% (Princeton). Each exclusive premise has 2 models, inclusive 3; a pair of inclusive gives 5.
limits: Cited findings; the explanation (limited working memory) is not directly tested here.
agent_relevance: An LLM is not limited by working memory in the same way, so these error patterns may not carry over. Test directly before copying the human pattern.

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste & Linzen (2024) A systematic comparison of syllogistic reasoning in humans and language models
finding: PaLM 2 models of several sizes on syllogisms with chain of thought. Larger models are more accurate than humans, but still make systematic errors, some mirror human ones (order of terms, syllogistic fallacies). Larger models fit an mReasoner-like deliberative profile more.
numbers: Human data from Ragni et al. 2019: 139 participants, each answered each syllogism once, human accuracy about 50%. Best LM accuracy about 75%. Principal component 1 of mReasoner behaviour explains 77% of variance and loads on System 2. Control analysis zeroing the correct answers: component 1 still correlates 0.6 with the System 2 parameter. LM accuracy on the 'nothing follows' answer close to 0%.
limits: PaLM 2 only (plus Llama 2 in appendix); zero-shot chain of thought; mReasoner mapping is by projection and is an interpretation. Larger models somewhat more prone to fallacies.
agent_relevance: LMs also drop 'nothing follows'. Our harvest and select steps should add an explicit 'no valid conclusion' candidate and test it by counterexample search.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt & Bernardi (2024) A systematic analysis of large language models as soft reasoners: the case of syllogistic inferences
finding: Study of Pythia and LLaMA models on syllogisms with believable and unbelievable conclusions and multi-premise chains. Models show content effects and avoid 'no valid conclusion'. In-context examples do not fix this; supervised fine-tuning does. The atmosphere heuristic predicts model output well.
numbers: Human accuracy in the comparison: 44.63% on valid and 40.97% on invalid syllogisms (from Khemlani and Johnson-Laird, 2012). Atmosphere theory predicts 92% of LLaMA zero-shot chain-of-thought correct valid conclusions and 82.97% of its errors on invalid and 62.79% on valid schemas. Fine-tuned models near ceiling on both valid and invalid. In-context examples made models more contradictory.
limits: Open-weight models of 2024 vintage; small fine-tuning set results do not tell about frontier models; atmosphere account is a correlation with output not mechanism.
agent_relevance: Shows a weak model drifts to heuristic answers (atmosphere). The remedy found was a form-focused procedure (fine-tuning), consistent with code-driven checks rather than prompt hints.
